Mechanics of Breathing

1. Definition and Overview

The mechanics of breathing refers to the process by which the lungs expand and contract to facilitate the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide. This process is essential for the survival of all living organisms. The incidence of breathing disorders is high, with millions of people worldwide suffering from conditions such as asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and pneumonia. The etiology of breathing disorders can be attributed to a variety of factors, including:
  • Genetic predisposition
  • Environmental factors, such as air pollution and smoking
  • Infections, such as pneumonia and tuberculosis
  • Chronic diseases, such as heart disease and diabetes

2. Classification / Types

The types of breathing can be classified into several categories, including:
Type Features Examples
Normal breathing Quiet, effortless breathing Healthy individuals
Deep breathing Slow, deep breaths Yoga, meditation, and relaxation techniques
Shallow breathing Rapid, shallow breaths Anxiety, stress, and respiratory disorders

3. Pathophysiology / Mechanism

The mechanism of breathing involves the following steps:
  1. The diaphragm contracts, increasing the volume of the thoracic cavity
  2. The intercostal muscles contract, further increasing the volume of the thoracic cavity
  3. Air enters the lungs, and the alveoli expand
  4. Oxygen diffuses into the bloodstream, and carbon dioxide diffuses out of the bloodstream
  5. The partial pressure of oxygen (pO2) is typically 75-100 mmHg, while the partial pressure of carbon dioxide (pCO2) is typically 35-45 mmHg

4. Clinical Features / Signs and Symptoms

The symptoms of breathing disorders can vary depending on the underlying condition. Cardinal symptoms include:
  • Dyspnea (shortness of breath)
  • Wheezing
  • Coughing
Early features may include:
  • Mild dyspnea
  • Wheezing
  • Coughing
Late features may include:
  • Severe dyspnea
  • Respiratory failure
  • Cardiac arrest

5. Diagnosis

The diagnosis of breathing disorders involves the following:
  • Clinical history
  • Physical examination
  • Laboratory tests, such as:
    • Arterial blood gas (ABG): pH 7.35-7.45, pO2 75-100 mmHg, pCO2 35-45 mmHg
    • Pulmonary function tests (PFTs): forced expiratory volume (FEV1) 80-120% of predicted, forced vital capacity (FVC) 80-120% of predicted
  • Imaging studies, such as chest X-rays and computed tomography (CT) scans

6. Management / Treatment

The treatment of breathing disorders involves the following:
  1. Medical management, including:
    • Bronchodilators: albuterol 2.5-5 mg inhalation q 4-6 hours
    • Corticosteroids: prednisone 20-50 mg oral q day
  2. Surgical management, including lung transplantation and other surgical interventions

7. Nursing Care

The nursing care of patients with breathing disorders involves the following:
  • Nursing assessment, including:
    • Respiratory rate and depth
    • Oxygen saturation
    • Lung sounds
  • NANDA nursing diagnoses, including:
    • Impaired gas exchange
    • Activity intolerance
    • Anxiety
  • Nursing interventions, including:
    • Oxygen therapy
    • Bronchodilator therapy
    • Pulmonary rehabilitation
  • Patient education, including:
    • Medication management
    • Breathing techniques
    • Exercise and activity

8. Complications

The complications of breathing disorders can include:
  • Respiratory failure
  • Cardiac arrest
  • Pneumonia
Emergency complications may include:
  • Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)
  • Cardiopulmonary arrest
Immediate management may include:
  • Oxygen therapy
  • Ventilatory support
  • Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR)

9. Mnemonics and Memory Aids

The following mnemonics can be used to remember key concepts:
  • RESPIRE: R - rate, E - effort, S - sounds, P - pulse, I - inspiratory, R - respiratory, E - expiratory
  • BREATHE: B - bronchodilators, R - respiratory rate, E - effort, A - anxiety, T - treatment, H - history, E - examination
  • OXYGEN: O - oxygen therapy, X - x-ray, Y - years, G - gas exchange, E - emergency, N - nursing

10. Key Points for NORCET Exam

The following are key points to remember for the NORCET exam:
  1. The mechanics of breathing involve the contraction and relaxation of the diaphragm and intercostal muscles
  2. The types of breathing include normal, deep, and shallow breathing
  3. The pathophysiology of breathing disorders involves the impairment of gas exchange and the development of respiratory failure
  4. The clinical features of breathing disorders include dyspnea, wheezing, and coughing
  5. The diagnosis of breathing disorders involves clinical history, physical examination, laboratory tests, and imaging studies
  6. The treatment of breathing disorders involves medical management, including bronchodilators and corticosteroids, and surgical management, including lung transplantation
  7. The nursing care of patients with breathing disorders involves nursing assessment, NANDA nursing diagnoses, and nursing interventions, including oxygen therapy and pulmonary rehabilitation
  8. The complications of breathing disorders can include respiratory failure, cardiac arrest, and pneumonia
  9. The mnemonics and memory aids can be used to remember key concepts, including RESPIRE, BREATHE, and OXYGEN
  10. The key points to remember for the NORCET exam include the mechanics of breathing, types of breathing, pathophysiology of breathing disorders, clinical features, diagnosis, treatment, nursing care, complications, and mnemonics and memory aids
  11. The common exam traps include confusing the types of breathing, misunderstanding the pathophysiology of breathing disorders, and failing to recognize the clinical features and complications of breathing disorders
  12. The most frequently asked question patterns include questions about the mechanics of breathing, types of breathing, and pathophysiology of breathing disorders
  13. The key values and normal ranges to remember include the partial pressure of oxygen (pO2) and the partial pressure of carbon dioxide (pCO2), which are typically 75-100 mmHg and 35-45 mmHg, respectively
  14. The memory tricks for key values and normal ranges include using mnemonics, such as RESPIRE and BREATHE, to remember the key concepts and values
